reasoning_traces.think:
Excitement is defined as the total variation of win probabilities over time, capturing how much the likelihood of winning fluctuates during a match. The formal definition E = TV(P₁(t)) + TV(P₂(t)) reflects that higher variability in win expectancy leads to greater excitement. This is grounded in stochastic modeling where win probabilities evolve based on Poisson processes for goal scoring. As the game progresses, if these probabilities swing widely—due to scoring events or momentum shifts—the total variation increases, indicating higher excitement. For example, in soccer, a low-scoring game with many lead changes will have high excitement because the win probability oscillates frequently. Conversely, a game where one team dominates early has low excitement due to minimal variation in win probability. The Poisson model allows for precise computation of win probabilities given current scores and time remaining. When applied to real-world data like FIFA 2006 games, betting market estimates provide empirical validation of the theoretical excitement measure. Total variation acts as a proxy for unpredictability, aligning with intuitive notions of excitement. The derivation assumes continuous win probability functions and applies to elimination rounds without draws. In cases involving draws, the definition expands to include draw probability terms. The key insight is that excitement is not just about final outcome but about the journey through changing expectations.
